## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

BODY
Start by reframing the issue: this is less a moral fight about who is lazy and more a coordination failure under changing schedules and ambiguous agreements. The aim is not to win the argument but to make commitments checkable and revisable.

First, separate standards from methods. Agree on what counts as done: dishes washed and put away, bins out before collection, bathroom wiped down weekly. Do not require everyone to do it the same way if the outcome is acceptable.

Second, make agreements observable. A shared note, whiteboard, or simple app should list who, what, by when, and what happens if it is missed. Vague promises like “I’ll do more” are what later become “that isn’t what I meant.” A short weekly or fortnightly check-in, even ten minutes, can catch drift before resentment hardens.

Third, address the avoidance directly but not as an accusation. Speak one-to-one: “I notice you’ve been pulling away from these conversations, and I don’t want to corner you. What would make them easier?” Offer alternatives: written async updates, a shorter meeting, a rotating facilitator, or a neutral third party. Avoidance may be about anxiety, resentment, schedule exhaustion, or feeling outvoted; you do not know until asked.

Fourth, do not let one person’s absence become a silent veto. If someone will not discuss, set a temporary default with an opt-out: a fair rotation, a paid cleaner if everyone agrees and can afford it, or a clear minimum each person handles independently. Shared money and shared spaces still require consent, so do not impose costs unilaterally.

Finally, if repeated attempts fail, consider mediation or a conversation about whether the living arrangement still works. The practical goal is fewer repeated disputes and a way to revise the deal when schedules change, not perfect harmony.
COMMITMENTS
I take this to be primarily a coordination and communication problem, not a diagnosis of anyone’s character. My proposed first move is a visible, reviewable chore agreement plus a short recurring check-in; that depends on at least two flatmates being willing to try a low-cost structure and on no one vetoing all conversation. I would treat the avoiding friend’s absence as information to investigate, not as consent to any particular arrangement. If the trial does not reduce ambiguity, I would next consider a neutral facilitator or a discussion about changing the living arrangement; that step depends on lease terms, willingness, and whether anyone can afford to move or hire help. I am not assuming a cleaner is affordable, that all three want to stay, or that past resentment can be waved away. Unresolved: whether the avoidance stems from anxiety, resentment, schedule mismatch, or something outside the flat, and whether previous agreements have already made a new system feel punitive. A proposed test: for two weeks, use a shared board or calendar that defines each chore as outcome, deadline, and fallback, and hold a fifteen-minute weekly check-in; relevance is that it would show whether ambiguity or merely follow-through is the main obstacle. Success would be fewer “what did we agree” disputes and at least one missed task handled without a fight.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
